q: Why does chapter 2 add the Boolean as a new kind of value?
options: Comparisons need a result to return, and any value can then be tested for truth
Because numbers and strings cannot take part in decisions at all
Because Booleans replace integers everywhere in Python
Because an if statement accepts nothing except a Boolean
why: The chapter adds the Boolean value and with it the idea that any value can be tested for truth, which is what decisions in a program rely on.

q: What does every decision a program makes reduce to?
options: A choice between two indented blocks that is made before the program starts
A comparison operator typed by the programmer
why: Truth is the currency of flow control: each decision ends up as a true or false value.

q: How are the two Boolean values spelled in Python?
options: true and false, all in lowercase
TRUE and FALSE, all in capitals
True and False, each with a capital first letter
The words yes and no in quotation marks
why: The Boolean values are written True and False with a capital letter, and a comparison produces one of them.

q: Boolean value: what does this program print?
code:
result = 5 > 2
print(type(result).__name__, result)
why: A comparison produces a Boolean value, so 5 > 2 is True and its type is bool.

q: Which of these values counts as false when Python tests it for truth?
options: '0', a string that holds the digit zero
'False', a string that holds the word False
why: None, False, zero and empty sequences are false, and an empty list is an empty sequence; a non-empty string is true whatever it says.

q: Truthiness: what does this program print?
code: print(bool(''), bool(' '), bool(0.0), bool([0]))
why: An empty string and 0.0 are false, while a string of one space and the list [0] are not empty, so they are true.

q: What does a comparison operator give back?
options: A Boolean value that answers a question about two values
The larger of the two values
A number that says how far apart the values are
A copy of the first value
why: Comparison operators ask a question about two values and answer with a Boolean value.

q: How does an equality comparison differ from assignment?
options: It stores the right value in the left name, just as one equals sign does
It asks whether the left value is larger, while one equals sign asks whether they are equal
It changes both values so that they become the same
It asks whether two values are the same, while a single equals sign stores a value under a name
why: An equality comparison asks whether two values are the same, which is a different question from what the single equals sign of an assignment does.

q: Which operator tests that two values are different?
why: The == and != operators compare values, and != is the one that is true when the values differ.

q: Equality: what does this program print?
why: 1 == 1.0 is True because == compares values, 'a' == 'A' is False because the letters differ, and [1, 2] != [1, 2] is False because the lists have equal contents.

q: What do the ordering comparisons ask about two values?
options: Whether they have the same type
why: Ordering comparisons ask which of two values comes first, and they combine with Boolean operators into longer conditions.

q: What is the difference between < and <=?
options: < is for numbers and <= is for text
<= is also true when the two values are equal, while < is not
< returns a Boolean and <= returns the larger value
There is none, both give the same result for every pair
why: The operators <, >, <= and >= compare order and return a Boolean value; the ones with an equals sign also accept equal values.

q: Ordering: what does this program print?
why: 3 < 3 is False, 3 <= 3 is True, 7 >= 8 is False and 10 > 9 is True.

q: How does Python read the chained comparison 1 < x < 10?
options: As (1 < x) < 10, comparing a Boolean with 10
As 1 < x and x < 10, with x evaluated once
As a syntax error, because only two values may be compared
why: Comparisons chain, so x < y <= z means x < y and y <= z, with y evaluated once.

q: Chained comparison: what does this program print?
why: With x equal to 5, 1 < x < 10 is True, 1 < x < 5 is False because 5 < 5 fails, and 10 > x >= 5 is True.

q: What do the operators and, or and not work on?
options: Only whole numbers, which they combine bit by bit
Only strings, which they join together
Only comparisons, never a plain value
Truth values, which they combine or invert, often together with comparisons
why: The Boolean operators combine truth values, and the chapter shows them mixed with comparisons in one expression.

q: Which three operators make up the Boolean operators of the chapter?
why: Each Boolean operator has a truth table in the chapter, and and, or and not together can express any condition a program needs.

q: In which case is an and expression false?
options: Only when both operands are false
When at least one operand is false
Only when the first operand is false
Only when the two operands differ
why: and is true only when both operands are true, so it is false as soon as one of them is false.

q: And operator: what does this program print?
code: print(True and True, True and False, False and False, not (True and False))
why: and gives True only for True and True, and not (True and False) inverts a False into True.

q: In which case is an or expression false?
options: When at least one operand is false
When exactly one operand is false
Only when both operands are false
why: or is true when either operand is true, so it is false only when both operands are false.

q: Or operator: what does this program print?
code: print(False or False, False or True, True or True, 0 < 1 or 1 < 0)
why: or is false only for False or False; the last one is True because 0 < 1 is True.

q: What does the not operator do?
options: Returns True whenever its operand is missing
Leaves a Boolean operand as it is and changes other values
Turns a true operand into false and a false one into true
Joins two values the way and does
why: not inverts a single Boolean value.

q: Not operator: what does this program print?
code: print(not True, not False, not not True, not 0, not 'x')
why: not True is False, not False is True, not not True is True, and not 0 is True because 0 is false while not 'x' is False because a non-empty string is true.

q: Why does the way a Boolean operator evaluates matter as much as its result?
options: Both operands are always evaluated, from right to left
The second operand is evaluated first and the first only when needed
The operators change the values of their operands
The second operand is sometimes never evaluated, so what it would do may not happen
why: The second operand of a Boolean operator is sometimes never evaluated at all, so the way of evaluating changes what a program does.

q: Which names end up in the list calls when this program has run?
code:
calls = []
def check(name, result):
    calls.append(name)
    return result
check('a', False) and check('b', True)
check('c', True) or check('d', False)
check('e', False) or check('f', True)
print(calls)
why: and skips its second operand after a false first one and or skips it after a true first one, so only b and d are never called.

q: What does the or operator return when its first operand is true?
options: The first operand itself, without evaluating the second
The Boolean True, whatever the operand was
The first operand, after evaluating the second one
why: and and or stop as soon as the answer is known and return an operand rather than a Boolean.

q: Short circuit: what does this program print?
code:
log = []
def f(v):
    log.append(v)
    return v
first = f(0) and f(1)
second = f(2) or f(3)
print(first, second, log)
why: 0 is false so and stops with 0 and never calls f(1); 2 is true so or stops with 2 and never calls f(3).

q: What does this fallback idiom print?
code:
name = ''
print(name or 'guest', 'Al' or 'guest', 'Al' and 'ok')
why: '' is false so or moves on to 'guest', 'Al' is true so or stops with it, and 'Al' and 'ok' returns its second operand 'ok'.

q: What does flow control decide?
options: Which lines run and in what order
Which names may hold a Boolean value
How the output of the program is formatted
why: Flow control decides which lines run and in what order, built from conditions and blocks.

q: Which two parts does every decision in a program need?
why: The chapter names a condition and a block as the two parts every decision needs.

q: Which of these can serve as the condition of an if statement?
options: Only a comparison, since only comparisons give Booleans
Only the written values True and False
Only a name that already holds a Boolean
Any expression, because Python evaluates it for its truth value
why: A condition is an expression evaluated for its truth value, and every value can be tested for truth.

q: Condition: what does this program print?
why: The empty list is false when tested for truth, so the if block is skipped and the else block runs.

q: How does Python know which lines belong to a block?
options: They are wrapped in curly braces
why: A block is a group of lines at the same indentation; Python uses indentation, not braces, to mark it.

q: Block: what does this program print?
code:
n = 1
out = []
if n > 2:
    out.append('a')
    out.append('b')
out.append('c')
print(out)
why: The two append lines are indented under the if, so they are skipped as a pair; the last append is not indented, so it always runs.

q: Which keywords build a branch?
why: Branches are built with if, else and elif.

q: What does an if statement do when its condition is false?
options: It skips its block and carries on after it
why: if runs its block only when its condition is true, and skips it otherwise.

q: If statement: what does this program print?
why: 7 is odd, so the first block is skipped; 7 > 3 is true, so 10 is added, giving 17.

q: When is the condition of an elif tested?
options: Only when every earlier condition in the chain was false
Every time the chain runs, right after the if
Only when the if condition was true
Only when the else block did not run
why: elif tests a further condition only when every earlier one was false.

q: Elif clause: what does this program print?
why: age < 5 is false and age < 12 is true, so that branch runs; because at most one branch of the chain runs, the later elif is never tested.

q: This program uses elif where a beginner might write a second if. What does it print?
code:
n = 15
out = []
if n % 3 == 0:
    out.append('three')
elif n % 5 == 0:
    out.append('five')
print(out)
why: 15 % 3 == 0 is true, and because at most one branch of the chain runs, the elif for five is never tested.

q: When does the block of an else clause run?
options: After every if block, whatever its condition was
Only when the if condition raised an error
When no earlier condition in the chain was true
When the last condition of the chain was true
why: else runs its block when no earlier condition in the chain was true.

q: Else clause: what does this program print?
why: 50 is not at least 90 and not at least 60, so no earlier condition is true and the else assigns 'C'.

q: What is the conditional expression form for?
options: Running several statements on one line
Repeating a block while a condition holds
Testing a value against several patterns at once
Choosing a value inside one expression instead of running a block
why: Some decisions choose a value rather than run a block, and the expression form is Python's answer for that case.

q: In the expression x if C else y, which part is evaluated first?
options: Both x and y, and then C picks one
why: The conditional expression evaluates the condition first and returns one of the two values.

q: Conditional expression: what does this program print?
code:
n = 7
label = 'even' if n % 2 == 0 else 'odd'
print(label, 'big' if n > 5 else 'small')
why: 7 % 2 == 0 is false, so the first expression gives 'odd', and 7 > 5 is true, so the second gives 'big'.

q: What does this program print, given that the condition is evaluated first?
code:
d = 0
print(10 / d if d else 'no division')
why: d is 0, which is false, so the condition picks the other value and 10 / d is never evaluated.

q: Why does an advanced course also look at forms beyond the chapter's if-elif chains?
options: If-elif chains no longer work in current Python
The newer forms always run faster than a chain
Current Python offers newer forms for the same decisions, and they can read better
Only the newer forms can produce Boolean values
why: An advanced course pairs the chapter's if-elif chains with the forms current Python offers for the same decisions.

q: What can pattern matching test that a plain equality comparison does not?
options: Only whether a value is a Boolean
Only how many characters a string has
Whether a value is stored in a variable
The shape of a value, such as a list of two items, as well as its value
why: Pattern matching tests a value's shape as well as its value, which elif chains can only imitate.

q: Since which Python version does the match statement exist?
why: The match statement has existed since Python 3.10 as the modern alternative to a long elif chain.

q: Match statement: what does this program print?
code:
def kind(cmd):
    match cmd:
        case 'go':
            return 'moving'
        case 'stop' | 'halt':
            return 'stopped'
        case _:
            return 'unknown'
print(kind('halt'), kind('go'), kind('jump'))
why: match compares the value with the case patterns in turn: 'halt' matches the pattern 'stop' | 'halt', 'go' matches its case, and 'jump' reaches the catch-all case.

q: What does this program print, given that a case pattern tests the shape of the value?
code:
def describe(p):
    match p:
        case [x, y]:
            return 'pair'
        case [x]:
            return 'single'
        case _:
            return 'other'
print(describe([1, 2]), describe([9]), describe('ab'), describe([1, 2, 3]))
why: The pattern [x, y] needs a sequence of exactly two items, [x] one item; a string is not treated as such a sequence and [1, 2, 3] has three items, so the last two reach the catch-all case.

q: What do the style conventions for conditions aim at?
options: Making conditions as short as possible in characters
Turning every condition into a comparison
why: Style guidance keeps conditions readable, and the conventions for Boolean tests are among the most often broken.

q: Which line follows PEP 8 for a Boolean variable named greeting?
why: PEP 8 advises testing a Boolean directly instead of comparing it to True with ==.

q: What does this program print, and what does it show about writing == True?
code:
greeting = 'hello'
print(bool(greeting), greeting == True)
why: A non-empty string is true when tested directly but is not equal to True, so a test written with == True can behave differently; PEP 8 advises testing directly.

q: What does the value None stand for in a program?
options: The number zero written as a keyword
An empty string with no characters at all
The Boolean value False under another name
why: None is the value that stands for the absence of a value; it is not zero, not an empty string and not False.

q: None value: what does this program print?
code: print(bool(None), None == False, type(None).__name__)
why: None counts as false when tested, but it is not equal to False, and its type is NoneType.

q: What does Python decide about every empty container when it is tested for truth?
options: It counts as true because the container exists
It raises an error because nothing can be tested
It counts as None, a special missing value
why: An empty list, tuple, string, dictionary or set is false, and a container with at least one item is true.

q: Sequence and collection: what does this program print?
code: print(len([10, 20, 30]), bool([]), bool({}), bool(set()), bool([0]))
why: len counts the three items; the empty list, dictionary and set are false, and [0] is true because it holds one item.

q: Which line only asks whether x holds 5, leaving x unchanged?
why: A double equals sign asks a question; a single equals sign stores a value, and the other two forms are not Python.

q: Equality versus assignment: what does this program print?
code:
x = 3
result = x == 5
x = 5
print(result, x == 5)
why: The comparison with 3 gives False and is stored; after the assignment x holds 5, so the second comparison is True.

q: What does the is operator compare?
options: Whether both sides are the very same object
Whether both sides hold values that look equal
Whether the left side is a kind of the right
Whether both sides print the same text
why: The operator is asks about identity, not about equal content.

q: Identity comparison: what does this program print?
code:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b, a is c)
why: Two separate lists with equal content are equal but not identical, whereas c is another name for the list a.

q: Why is 'Zebra' < 'apple' true in Python?
options: Python compares the lengths of the two strings first
Python puts uppercase words in front only for names
Python ignores case, and Z comes before a in its table
Capital letters have smaller code points than lowercase letters
why: Strings are compared by the code points of their characters, and every capital letter has a smaller code point than every lowercase letter.

q: String ordering: what does this program print?
code: print('apple' < 'banana', 'Zebra' < 'apple', 'abc' < 'ab', '10' < '9')
why: Comparison goes letter by letter by code point: a prefix is smaller than the longer string, and '1' is smaller than '9'.

q: How many operands does the not operator take?
options: Two, so it is a binary operator
Three, so it is a ternary operator
Any number, like a function call
One, so it is a unary operator
why: The word not stands in front of one operand, whereas and and or take two.

q: Binary and unary operators: what does this program print?
why: The minus sign is binary in 5 - 3 and unary in -(2 + 3); in 5 - -3 it is both, and subtracting -3 adds 3.

q: How many rows does the truth table of a Boolean operator with two operands have?
options: Two, one for True and one for False
Three, because None is a third operand value
Four, one for each pair of operand values
Six, one for each comparison operator
why: Each of the two operands can be True or False, so there are 2 x 2 = 4 combinations.

q: Truth table: what does this program print?
code:
rows = [(a, b) for a in (True, False) for b in (True, False)]
print([a and b for a, b in rows])
why: The pairs run through (True, True), (True, False), (False, True), (False, False), and and is true only for the first.

q: What does an and expression return when its first operand is false?
options: Always the Boolean False, whatever the operand was
The second operand, which is evaluated anyway
The first operand itself, not necessarily a Boolean
Always None, to mark the part that was skipped
why: and returns its first operand when that operand is false, so 0 and 5 is 0, not False.

q: Operand result: what does this program print?
code: print('' or 'default', 'x' and 'y', 0 and 5, [] or None)
why: or and and hand back one of their operands: the second of '' or 'default', the second of 'x' and 'y', the first of 0 and 5, and the second of [] or None.

q: What is a compound Boolean expression?
options: One built from comparisons joined by and, or and not
A comparison between two Boolean values only
A number that Python converts to True or False
Any statement whose block holds an if statement
why: Comparisons give Boolean values, and the Boolean operators combine them into one larger expression.

q: Boolean expression: what does this program print?
code:
age = 20
member = False
print(age >= 18 and member, age >= 18 or member, age < 18 or not member)
why: age >= 18 is true and member is false, so and gives False, or gives True, and age < 18 or not member is False or True.

q: In which order does Python apply the three Boolean operators?
options: or first, then and, then not
not first, then and, then or
and first, then or, then not
Left to right, all with the same priority
why: not binds most strongly, then and, and or binds least strongly.

q: Boolean precedence: what does this program print?
code: print(True or False and False, (True or False) and False, not True or True)
why: and is applied before or, so the first expression is True or (False and False); parentheses change the second, and not applies first in the third.

q: What does execution flow describe about a program?
options: How much time each statement needs when the program is running
Which statements run, in which order, and which are skipped
How many variables the program creates before it first stops
Which lines of the program the user typed in while it ran
why: Execution flow is the path through the program: what runs first, what runs next and what is skipped.

q: Which of these is a flow control statement?
options: An assignment that stores a value in a variable
An if statement with its elif and else parts
A call of print that shows a message on the screen
A comparison that gives True or False as its result
why: The if statement decides which other statements run; an assignment, a call and a comparison do not.

q: What does a flow control statement do that an assignment does not?
options: It stores a value under a name in memory
It produces a value for the line that follows
It converts a value to another type before use
It decides which other statements run
why: A flow control statement is a compound statement that chooses among blocks of statements; an assignment only stores a value.

q: In the textbook's picture, what does the finger do at an if statement whose condition is false?
options: It stops moving until the condition becomes true
It enters the block and stops at its last line
It goes back to the first line of the program
It jumps past the block to the first line after it
why: Program execution is the finger on the current line, and a false condition makes it skip the whole block.

q: Program execution: what does this program print?
code:
log = ['start']
if 0:
    log.append('inside')
log.append('end')
print(log)
why: The condition 0 is false, so the line inside the block is never executed and the others run in order.

q: In a flowchart of an if statement, what does the diamond stand for?
options: The condition, with one exit for true and one for false
The block, drawn once for each line it holds
The start of the program, where the finger rests
The end of the program, after the last line
why: Branching points are drawn as diamonds; the arrows that leave one lead to the steps for true and false.

q: Which shape does a flowchart use for an ordinary step such as printing a message?
options: A rounded rectangle, as for the start
why: Steps are rectangles, branching points are diamonds, and start and end are rounded rectangles.

q: What happens when a line is indented for no reason, with no block opened before it?
options: The line is skipped without any message
Python ignores the extra spaces and runs the line
The line becomes a comment on the previous line
why: Indentation is part of the syntax, so unexpected indentation is an IndentationError (unexpected indent).

q: Indentation: what does this program print?
options: SyntaxError raised by the if line
No output, since compile does not run the code
why: A colon must be followed by an indented block; the unindented print is rejected as an IndentationError, a kind of SyntaxError.

q: What does the textbook call the block of code that follows an if statement?
why: The textbook calls the block after if the if clause and the block after else the else clause.

q: What must the header of a clause end with?
why: The header begins with a keyword and ends with a colon; without it Python reports a SyntaxError.

q: Why can a program not use if as the name of a variable?
options: It is a built-in function that cannot be replaced by anything
Variable names are not allowed to contain two letters or fewer
It is a type name that Python keeps for whole numbers only
It is a keyword, a word reserved by the language
why: Keywords are reserved and cannot be used as ordinary names; if = 3 is a SyntaxError.

q: Keyword: what does this program print?
code:
import keyword
print(keyword.iskeyword('if'), keyword.iskeyword('true'), keyword.iskeyword('True'))
why: if and True are keywords, but the lowercase true is not reserved, so it is simply an unknown name.

q: How does a chain of if, elif and else differ from separate if statements?
options: The chain runs at most one block, whereas separate statements may all run
The chain tests every condition, whereas separate statements stop at the first true one
The chain can only contain two conditions, whereas separate statements can contain more
The chain runs faster in every case, whereas separate statements give different answers
why: In a chain the first true condition wins and the rest are not tested; separate ifs are tested independently.

q: Branch chain: what does this program print?
why: The two separate ifs both run, giving A and B; the chain that follows runs only its first true branch, adding x.

q: What does the operator := do in (limit := 10) > 5?
options: It compares limit with 10 and gives True to the comparison
It declares limit as a constant that cannot change later
It assigns 10 to limit and gives the value 10 to the comparison
It creates an empty limit and tests whether 10 is larger
why: An assignment expression stores the value in the name and also yields it, so the comparison sees 10.

q: Assignment expression: what does this program print?
code:
if (size := len('Alice')) > 3:
    print(size, size > 3)
why: The condition stores len('Alice') in size while testing it, so the block can use size afterwards.

q: What does the pattern 401 | 403 | 404 in a case accept?
options: Only the value 401, the other two are comments
The sum of the three numbers, which is 1208
Only a value that equals all three at once
Any of the three values, with one shared block
why: The bars join alternatives, so the case matches when the subject equals any of them.

q: Case pattern: what does this program print?
code:
status = 403
match status:
    case 400:
        print('bad')
    case 401 | 403 | 404:
        print('not allowed')
    case _:
        print('other')
why: 403 does not equal 400, but it is one of the alternatives of the second case, so that block runs.

q: What does case _: do in a match statement?
options: It matches only the value written as an underscore
It matches any value that no earlier case matched
It marks a case that is skipped on purpose
It matches the empty value None and nothing else
why: The wildcard always succeeds and binds no name, so as the last case it plays the part of else.

q: Wildcard pattern: what does this program print?
code:
def f(c):
    match c:
        case 'go':
            return 'moving'
        case _:
            return 'unknown'
print(f('go'), f('dance'), f(None))
why: Only 'go' matches the first case; every other value, even None, falls through to the wildcard.

q: Which subject does the case ['go', direction] match?
options: The string 'go north', binding direction to 'north'
The list ['go'], binding direction to an empty string
why: A sequence pattern needs a sequence of the same length, and a string is never matched by it.

q: Sequence pattern: what does this program print?
code:
def f(cmd):
    match cmd:
        case ['go', d]:
            return 'go ' + d
        case ['quit']:
            return 'bye'
        case _:
            return 'no match'
print(f(['go', 'north']), f(['quit']), f('quit'), f(['go']))
options: go north bye bye no match
go north no match no match no match
go north bye no match no match
go north bye no match go
why: Only lists of the right length match, and the string 'quit' does not match the sequence pattern ['quit'].

q: When is the block of case (x, y) if x == y: selected?
options: When the subject is a pair and its two items are equal
When the subject is a pair, whatever its items are
When the subject is a pair whose items are both 1
When x is assigned the value y before the match starts
why: The pattern must match and then the guard condition must be true.

q: Guard: what does this program print?
code:
def f(p):
    match p:
        case (x, y) if x == y:
            return 'diagonal'
        case (x, y):
            return 'pair'
        case _:
            return 'other'
print(f((2, 2)), f((2, 3)), f(5))
why: (2, 2) passes the guard, (2, 3) matches the second case, and 5 is not a pair.

q: What makes match a soft keyword?
options: It is reserved everywhere, but only in recent versions of Python
It is reserved only where a match statement uses it
It can be spelled in capital letters as well as lowercase ones
It can only be used for variables that hold a text value
why: Soft keywords are reserved in a context only, so older programs with a variable called match still work.

q: Soft keyword: what does this program print?
code:
import keyword
match = 3
print(match, keyword.issoftkeyword('match'), keyword.iskeyword('match'))
why: match works as an ordinary variable name, and keyword reports it as a soft keyword but not as a hard one.

q: Which test for None follows PEP 8?
why: PEP 8 asks for is or is not when comparing with singletons such as None.

q: What does this program print, and why does PEP 8 prefer is None?
why: Equality can be customised by the object, so == None may be True for an object that is not None; is cannot be customised.

q: Which test for a non-empty list follows PEP 8?
why: PEP 8 says to use the fact that empty sequences are false instead of testing the length.

q: Emptiness test: what does this program print?
options: empty empty has items has items
empty has items has items has items
has items has items has items has items
why: An empty list and an empty string are false; the tuple (0,) and the dictionary each hold an item, so they are true.

q: How many spaces per indentation level does PEP 8 ask for?
why: PEP 8 asks for four spaces per indentation level.

q: What does Python do with code that mixes tabs and spaces inconsistently for indentation?
options: It can reject it, for example with a TabError
It always converts the tabs into four spaces silently
It runs it and reports a warning at the end
It treats every tab as exactly one space
why: A TabError is raised when the meaning would depend on the width of a tab, which is why spaces are preferred.

q: What does a complete worked program show that an isolated example cannot?
options: How fast each line of the program can be executed
How to type the program without making any typing mistakes
How the ideas depend on each other
How the interpreter is installed and started on a computer
why: A comparison feeds a condition, the condition selects a block, and the block assigns a variable that a later line uses.

q: Which of these is a decision pattern from the worked programs?
options: The loop, which repeats a block of lines
The import, which loads a module into the program
The toggle, which reverses a Boolean variable
The function, which gives a block of lines a name
why: The worked programs contain the toggle, the case-insensitive test, the unassigned name and the input guard.

q: What does flag = not flag do?
options: It tests whether flag is true and prints it
It sets flag to the opposite Boolean value
It sets flag to False whatever it was before
It raises an error because flag is used before it is set
why: The right side is evaluated first from the old value, and the negation is stored back under the same name.

q: Toggle: what does this program print?
code:
on = False
seen = [on]
on = not on
seen.append(on)
on = not on
seen.append(on)
print(seen)
why: Each use of not on the stored value reverses it: False, then True, then False again.

q: Why does the capacity program test unit == 'TB' or unit == 'tb'?
options: So that the unit is converted to uppercase for later use
So that the program stops when the unit is mistyped
So that either test may be skipped because it is slower
So that both spellings of the unit are accepted
why: The or operator makes the condition true for either spelling, so the user may type the unit in uppercase or lowercase.

q: Case-insensitive test: what does this program print?
why: Only the exact spellings 'TB' and 'tb' pass; the mixed spelling 'Tb' and the other unit do not.

q: In the first version of the capacity program, why does the unit 'KB' end in a NameError?
options: The unit KB is not a valid string in Python
The condition unit == 'KB' raises the error itself
No branch ran, so discrepancy was never assigned
The variable discrepancy is deleted by the else clause
why: The variable is assigned only inside the if and elif clauses, so for other units it does not exist when it is used.

q: Unassigned name: what does this program print?
why: Neither condition is true for 'KB', so discrepancy is never created and print raises a NameError.

q: What does the else clause sys.exit('You must enter TB or GB') achieve?
options: It assigns a default value so that the program can go on
It converts the unit to uppercase and tests it a second time
It shows a clear message and ends the program
It prints a traceback and keeps running the later lines
why: The guard turns a confusing NameError later on into a clear message at the place where the input is rejected.

q: Input guard: what does this program print?
options: SystemExit: You must enter TB or GB
You must enter TB or GB
why: sys.exit raises SystemExit, and its code is the message string; here the exception is caught and the code printed.

q: Why should a learner read the last line of an error report first?
options: It lists every line that the program has executed so far
It always shows the line that must be changed in the program
It counts the errors found and sorts them by importance
It names the kind of error and gives its message
why: The last line says what happened; the lines above it show where execution was.

q: Which kind of error says that an operation was applied to values of the wrong types?
why: TypeError is raised when an operation or function is applied to an object of inappropriate type.

q: How does an exception differ from a syntax error?
options: It is detected before any line of the program is read
It is detected while the program runs, not when the text is read
It can only come from a mistake in the indentation
It always stops the program in the same way, whatever the code
why: Exceptions arise only when execution reaches the line, whereas a syntax error is found when the parser reads the text.

q: Exception: what does this program print?
why: The faulty line is inside a block that is never executed, so no exception arises.

q: What does the SyntaxError for the line if x = 3: tell the programmer?
options: The variable x has no value yet
The text of the program is not valid Python
The number 3 is not allowed in a condition
The program ran out of memory while running
why: A SyntaxError is raised by the parser when the text does not follow the grammar; the condition needs == here.

q: SyntaxError: what does this program print?
options: No output, since compile does not run the code
why: compile reads the text only, and a single equals sign in a condition is a syntax error, found before x is looked up.

q: A program uses the word true in lowercase. Which error does Python report?
why: The lowercase true is not a keyword, only a name that has no value.

q: NameError: what does this program print?
why: The message of a NameError always has the shape name, the missing name in quotation marks, is not defined.

q: Why does 3 < '4' raise a TypeError instead of giving an answer?
options: Strings that hold digits may never be compared with anything
The operator < works only on strings and never on numbers
Python will not guess how to order a number and a string
Python first converts both sides to strings and then fails
why: Converting either side would hide a mistake, so the language refuses and reports both types.

q: TypeError: what does this program print?
why: An order comparison between an integer and a string is not supported.

q: Which operations raise a ZeroDivisionError when the second operand is zero?
options: Only the true division operator, written with a slash
Multiplication and exponentiation by a power of zero
why: A division or modulo operation with zero as the second argument raises the error.

q: ZeroDivisionError: what does this program print?
why: 10 // 2 is 5 and 7 // 7 is 1; the division by zero is caught and replaced by the word zero.

q: Which line of a traceback names the kind of error?
options: The first line, Traceback (most recent call last):
The line in the middle of the report
Every line except the last one
why: The last line gives the kind and the message; the lines above show how execution got there.

q: What does the first line of a traceback say?
options: The name of the file that was run
why: Every traceback of an uncaught error starts with Traceback (most recent call last):.
